solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

indicators.note: the outer word gathers the other in, holding it inside

blocks.note: H = hot, as on a tap

annotation.surface: Someone collecting scorching gravel off a sunbaked path.
annotation.walkthrough: SINGLE opens after its first letter to take in H.
annotation.definitionFit: Shingle is the loose rounded gravel found on beaches.

entries.clue: Random rot seen partly rising in tumult (5)

indicators.note: only part of the words is used
in a down clue, rising means read from bottom to top

blocks.note: the letters M ROT sit at the end of RandoM ROT, then S from seen

annotation.surface: Something decaying at random, glimpsed amid turmoil.
annotation.walkthrough: Read RandoM ROT Seen from the bottom up in this down clue and STORM appears.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a violent outburst of weather or of feeling is a tumult.

blocks.note: a public convenience is a public toilet in Britain

annotation.surface: A grumble about something irritating found in the lavatory.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one phrase, but 'in' is simply kept as IN and set before the word for toilet. In Britain a public convenience is a public toilet.
annotation.definitionFit: An inconvenience is something that causes annoyance or trouble.

indicators.note: what we hear is the sound of a word, not its spelling

blocks.note: to have suspected something is to have had a hunch about it

annotation.surface: Rumour has it a caller was under suspicion.
annotation.walkthrough: GUESSED and GUEST are pronounced identically; 'suspected' looks like it describes the visitor but only supplies the sound.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone staying at your home or attending as your invitee is your visitor.

entries.clue: Complete part of shipment I received (6)

indicators.note: the answer is only part of the words that follow

annotation.surface: Someone confirming they got all of their delivery.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer spans three words, starting in the tail of 'shipment' and ending at the front of 'received'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain adjective synonym: nothing is missing from something whole.

indicators.note: something that revolves turns round, so the word is turned back to front

annotation.surface: An Irishman named Paddy sheltering a rebel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Paddy' looks like an Irishman and 'harbours' like a verb; in fact paddy is British slang for a fit of temper, as is strop, and harbours is the plural noun.
annotation.definitionFit: A strop and a paddy are both British words for a sulky fit of temper.

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so take the final letter of each word

blocks.note: shall = will, both marking the future
the final letters of gO and extincT

annotation.surface: A gloomy forecast that some crop is doomed to die out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' reaches back over both 'go' and 'extinct', giving one letter from each.
annotation.definitionFit: A shallot is a small onion-like vegetable.

entries.clue: Check flower’s appearance in new form (13)

blocks.note: to rein in is to check or restrain

annotation.surface: Inspecting how a bloom looks after it has been restyled.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's after 'flower' stands for 'has' and simply joins the pieces to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Reincarnation is rebirth, appearing again in a new body or form.

entries.clue: Caters first of parties with 50 per cent off ciders (7)

indicators.note: take the first letter of the word that follows
half the word is removed, here its first half

blocks.note: and = with, as in bread and butter
CIDERS with its first three letters, half of six, taken off

annotation.surface: A caterer at a party knocking half price off the ciders.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Caters' looks like a noun for the people supplying the party; it is the verb, as in caters to someone's whims.
annotation.definitionFit: To pander to someone is to cater to their wishes, usually too readily.

indicators.note: letters handed out in a new order

annotation.surface: Hector organising how the food supplies get handed out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Arrangement of rations' reads as one phrase, but 'of' only joins the definition to the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: An orchestration is an arrangement, of music for an orchestra or of events.

entries.clue: Title of man going around new church (7)

indicators.note: the first word goes round the next, enclosing it

annotation.surface: A man's title being passed round a newly built church.
annotation.walkthrough: N slips in between the second and third letters of MISTER.
annotation.definitionFit: A minster is a large or important church, such as York Minster.

indicators.note: the answer is hidden inside the words before it

annotation.surface: The streaming service's lenders keeping cash out of sight.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the gap between the two words; 'Hulu' is there only for its last two letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Lucre is money, usually with a sense of greed, as in filthy lucre.

entries.clue: Come out and come together after finale of Pride (6)

indicators.note: the piece named first is placed after the one named second
the finale is the end, so take the last letter

blocks.note: to merge is to come together

annotation.surface: Coming out and uniting at the close of a Pride march.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is about coming out at Pride, which makes 'Pride' look thematic; it only supplies its last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: to appear from hiding or from inside something, and the surface's coming-out sense fits too.

annotation.surface: An engineer is kept busy even as the years advance.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Getting on' looks like getting along with someone; here it means growing old.
annotation.definitionFit: Engaged means busy, as a phone line or a toilet is.

entries.clue: Horses for example upset flying geese (3-4)

indicators.note: set upside down, which in a down clue reverses the letters
the letters fly about into a new order

annotation.surface: Horses spooked by a skein of geese overhead.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Upset' reverses EG to GE, and 'flying' scrambles GEESE; the two indicators each govern only the word beside them.
annotation.definitionFit: Gee-gee is a childish British word for a horse.

indicators.note: to remove something is to take it away, so the letter for current is taken out of the plots

blocks.note: I is the symbol for electric current

annotation.surface: Schemes to strip the cash out of banks and vaults.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plots' looks like a verb; it is the noun, the storylines of books.
annotation.definitionFit: Stores are places where goods are deposited and kept.

entries.clue: Five love to board wagon and frolic (6)

indicators.note: to board is to get on inside, so these letters go into the other word

blocks.note: V is the Roman numeral for five
love = nil = O, as in tennis

annotation.surface: Five tennis players climbing on to a wagon for some fun.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Love' is the tennis score nil, which crosswords write as the letter O; 'board' is the verb, climbing aboard.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: both mean to leap about playfully.

annotation.surface: Dirt left behind by a disagreeable foreigner.
annotation.walkthrough: 'European' looks like a person in the story; it only contributes its abbreviation E.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain noun synonym: ingrained dirt on a surface.

entries.clue: Stop next to snake for paving material (7)

indicators.note: the two pieces sit side by side, in the order given

annotation.surface: Halting beside a snake stretched out on the road surface.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue names the stop first, but 'next to' lets the snake come first in the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Asphalt is the tarry material used to surface roads.

blocks.note: the sense here is set down heavily, with a thud
an informal British word for inferior wine

annotation.surface: Someone sneering at an inexpensive bottle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Put down' reads as disparage, as if mocking the wine; it means set down with a thump.
annotation.definitionFit: Plonk means both to set down heavily and, in Britain, cheap wine.

entries.clue: Carries infant with ease we hear (5)

indicators.note: what we hear is the sound of a word, not its spelling

blocks.note: a tot is a small child
ease sounds like the letters ES, said as 'eez'

annotation.surface: A parent effortlessly carrying a small child.
annotation.walkthrough: The sound indicator applies only to 'ease', not to 'infant'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym, originally American: to tote a bag is to carry it about, hence the tote bag.

indicators.note: the letters go mad and rearrange

annotation.surface: Altar servers losing their minds and needing medical attention.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Going' belongs to the fodder even though 'going crazy' reads as a single phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: A gynaecologist is a doctor specialising in women's reproductive health.

blocks.note: a verb, as in getting a salad, a wound or a shop window ready
a noun, clothing of a given kind, as in evening wear

annotation.surface: Laying out an outfit ready to wear.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Prepare' can also point to clothes (getting dressed), which lets the two senses read as one instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Dress means to prepare (a salad, a wound) and also clothing.

blocks.note: ta is British informal for thanks

annotation.surface: Gratitude shown to the bosses for the company's sales.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turnover' is a business's total sales, not a pastry or staff churn.
annotation.definitionFit: Takings are the money a shop or business takes in, its turnover.
